To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the thin carbon layer at carbon fiber/cement interfaces is a promising approach to enhance the thermoelectric properties and to develop new thermoelectric materials; (2) CFRCs with thin carbon layers are promising for harvesting ambient energy from the urban areas and roads; (3) CFRCs are promising for waste heat harvesting in cement industry.
the pyrolytic thin layer on carbon fiber surface is responsible for the high power factor and the low thermal conductivity, which results in a high figure of merit.

the pyrolytic layer at the fiber/matrix interface of CFRCs can enhance thermoelectric properties, resulting in high power factor and thermoelectric figure or merit, which are comparable to those of oxide thermoelectric compounds.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new class of thermoelectric materials based on cement composites with carbon fiber as the reinforcement.
the development of a novel class of CFRCs with a pyrolytic thin layer at the carbon fiber cement interface, which exhibit high thermoelectric properties.
the development of new materials for energy harvesting and conversion applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pyrolytic layer is a good choice for enhancing the thermoelectric properties and for the development of CFRCs as a new class of thermoelectric materials.
the pyrolytic layer at the carbon fiber cement interface can enhance the thermoelectric performance of CFRCs.
CFRCs are promising for thermoelectric applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pyrolytic thin carbon layers on carbon fibers are effective in increasing the power factor of CFRCs and the thermoelectric figure-of-merit is comparable to that of typical thermionic oxide materials.
the thermoelectric properties can be significantly enhanced by a thin carbon layer formed at the fiber/matrix interface.
pyrolytic layer can be a promising candidate as a new type of thermoelectric material, with the advantages of low cost, high mechanical strength and easy fabrication.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pyrolytic thin layer at the carbon fiber cement interface can be used to enhance the thermoelectric properties and thus to improve the performance of CFRCs for waste heat harvesting.
CFRCs with a pyrolytic layer are promising for thermoelectric applications.
